title: As-Samad, the Eternal Refuge
hookLine: the Eternal Refuge, whom all need (112:2)
tomorrow: asking God for the impossible: bold, or rude?

cards: Some words break translation apps. Type in the word some languages have for missing a place you've never been, and you get back a whole sentence. The second line of al-Ikhlas has a word like that.

In Arabic it's short: Allahu as-Samad. Pickthall, translating it, needed a phrase: "Allah, the eternally Besought of all!" Other translators reached for other words: eternal, refuge, the one everyone depends on.

teach.b: Maybe all of them. Commentators on the Qur'an have read As-Samad two ways, and English can only carry one picture at a time.
In one reading, As-Samad is the one everyone turns to, the place you go when you need something. That's Pickthall's Besought of all: asked, by all.
In the other, As-Samad is the one who needs nothing, who doesn't run low or wear out. That's where eternal comes from. Put the two together and the puzzle solves itself.
Only someone who needs nothing can be the refuge of everything. A friend who needs you back is a good friend. A refuge for all can't be running low.
The next line says it plainly: "He begetteth not nor was begotten." No one to lean on, no one to hand things off to. And here's the line worth telling a friend tonight.
The Qur'an is just as plain about our side of it: "O mankind! Ye are the poor in your relation to Allah."
Poor there means needy. Everyone. In this picture, needing isn't a failure or a weak moment.
It's simply true of every person, and As-Samad is the address where all of it is meant to go.

how: Muslims recite al-Ikhlas, with its line Allahu as-Samad, in prayer, and may call on Allah by His Names in personal du'a, as in ya Samad.

o: the one who forgives every sin a person regrets
the one who rules over every king on the earth
the one everyone turns to, who needs nothing

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the one who needs nothing, never runs low
every person is needy before Allah

s: needing help is a sign your faith is weak
the Qur'an says all people are needy before Allah. As-Samad is where that need goes.
As-Samad is in the second line of al-Ikhlas
Allahu as-Samad: in Pickthall, Allah, the eternally Besought of all.
translators all render As-Samad the same way
Pickthall needed a phrase; others chose eternal or refuge. the word holds more than one picture.

games.q: your friend's grandpa refuses help with his groceries: 'i don't need anybody.' your friend asks what to say to him. what fits As-Samad?
o: needing isn't weakness: in this picture everyone needs, and only God needs nothing.
respect it: the strongest people manage alone and never ask.
carry them anyway without a word; actions say it better.
games.why: the Qur'an calls every person needy before Allah. As-Samad says the one who needs nothing is the one all turn to, so needing is just being human.

practice: Write one line by hand: something you need this week that you can't make on your own, a yes, a calm night, someone's patience. Look at it for the sit without fixing it or apologizing for it.
If you make du'a, the Name is right there: ya Samad.

wordCard.voice: As-Samad. The Eternal Refuge: the one all creation turns to, who needs nothing back. Line two of al-Ikhlas.

orig.note: Arabic: the Eternal Refuge, the one all turn to. it appears in al-Ikhlas's second line.

carryVoice: For the road: all need him, says line two, and needing isn't failing. See you tomorrow.
